question.q: Cellars turn grams of sugar per litre into potential alcohol by dividing by a single figure, close enough for planning a harvest. Give that divisor.
accept: seventeen grams of sugar per litre
about 17 grams of sugar per litre
question.exp: Stoichiometry alone would ask for about fifteen and a half grams a litre, since a gram of sugar yields at most 0.51 grams of ethanol. A real ferment returns only about ninety-two per cent of that, because some of the sugar goes to glycerol, biomass and the ferment's own acids, so the sugar actually needed for each per cent climbs to a shade under seventeen and cellars round it. Two hundred and twenty grams a litre therefore points at around thirteen per cent, which is why a refractometer reading at the vineyard gate is enough to say whether a lot will need correcting before it is picked.

question.q: Squeezed hard at the end of the press cycle, a red picks up a green, bitter drying quality that a gentle cycle avoids altogether. Which fraction of the wine's tannin has just been added?
question.exp: Seed tannins are smaller, more heavily decorated with gallic acid and markedly more bitter than the tannins in the skin, and the seeds only give them up once there is alcohol in the vat or a press has cracked them. It is why press fractions are kept apart and tasted before any of them is blended back, and why a slow press and an intact seed are worth the extra hours.

findings.claim: The explanation says the ratio of 4-ethylphenol to its partner 4-ethylguaiacol is 'roughly constant, which is why a laboratory can report one figure and a cellar can act on it.'
findings.because: The ratio is not constant. It changes with grape variety and with how much p-coumaric acid versus ferulic acid the wine starts with. A survey of Brazilian reds found that 4-EP:4-EG ran from 1.37 to 21.98. It was higher in Cabernet Sauvignon, and the paper cites published ratios of 10:1 for Cabernet Sauvignon and 8:1 for Merlot. Laboratories such as ETS report both compounds separately for exactly this reason. The rest of the question and the key (4-ethylphenol) are correct.
findings.fix: Replace the last sentence of exp with: "Its partner, 4-ethylguaiacol, reads as smoke and clove rather than farmyard. The ratio between the two varies widely with the grape and the wine's hydroxycinnamic acids (roughly 8 to 10 to one in Cabernet and Merlot, much lower in some other wines), which is why a laboratory usually reports both."
findings.verifyReason: I checked the question (c-fzvm469u). The key and the accept list are right: 4-ethylphenol is the Brett phenol that gives the horse-and-farmyard note. The explanation's last sentence is wrong, though. It says the 4-EP:4-EG ratio is "roughly constant, which is why a laboratory can report one figure." I opened the PMC paper myself. It measured ratios in Brazilian reds running from 1.37 to 21.98, and it says that matches the 1.6 to 38 range reported by Pollnitz et al. (2000) and Henschke et al. (2004). It also found a statistically significant difference between Cabernet Sauvignon (9.24) and Merlot (7.51). It cites 10:1 for Cabernet and 8:1 for Merlot (Pollnitz), 8:1 for Bordeaux (Chatonnet 1992) and about 9:1 for Chilean wines. It puts the variation down to how much of each precursor the wine has, which depends on region and grape variety. A ratio that varies more than tenfold is not roughly constant, and it is why laboratories report both compounds. The examiner's replacement is accurate and keeps the rest of the explanation as it is.
findings.finalFix: Its partner, 4-ethylguaiacol, reads as smoke and clove rather than farmyard. The ratio between the two varies widely with the grape and the wine's hydroxycinnamic acids (roughly 8 to 10 to one in Cabernet and Merlot, much lower in some other wines), which is why a laboratory usually reports both.

question.q: Asked to confirm Brettanomyces in a suspect barrel, a laboratory reports the volatile phenol that carries the horse-and-farmyard note, in micrograms per litre. Name that compound.
question.exp: The yeast decarboxylates a hydroxycinnamic acid that every red already carries and then reduces the product, and the analysis is far more reliable than a plate count because the cells can be scarce while the compound is not. Its partner reads as smoke and clove rather than farmyard, and the ratio between the two is roughly constant, which is why a laboratory can report one figure and a cellar can act on it.
